title: Topic vs main idea
blurb: Tell the topic from the main idea, find the sentence that states the main idea of a multi-paragraph passage, and reject options that are too narrow or too broad.
question: A three-paragraph HESI A2 passage describes a clinic's ten-minute walking meetings, reports that staff feel more alert, and notes that meetings now end on time. The question asks 'What is the main idea of the passage?' One choice repeats the line about alertness; another says exercise improves health. Which choice is the main idea, and how do you rule out the other two?

teach.body: Formally, the topic is the subject of a passage, the main idea is the central point the author makes about that subject, and supporting details are the facts, examples, statistics, reasons and anecdotes that explain or prove that point. In plain English: the topic answers 'What is it about?', the main idea answers 'What is the author saying about it?', and the details answer 'How do we know?'

rows.label: Example
values: They boost focus at no time cost

teach.caption: If an option is a single phrase with no claim, it is a topic, not a main idea.

teach.body:
(1) Many clinics now hold short 'walking huddles' instead of seated staff meetings. Once or twice a week, a team spends ten minutes walking a loop around the parking lot while the manager runs through the agenda.

(2) The benefits show up quickly. Staff at one Ohio clinic said the walks left them more alert for afternoon appointments. Managers noticed that the meetings also ended on time, because no one wanted to keep circling the lot once the agenda was done. Employees with mobility limits join by phone, so no one is left out.

(3) Walking huddles are not right for every conversation: private patient matters still belong indoors. But for routine updates, busy health teams are finding that a walking huddle can turn an ordinary meeting into a small boost in energy and focus without adding time to the day.

teach.h: How the model passage is built

root.label: Main idea (end of paragraph 3)
root.sub: Walking huddles boost focus without adding time

teach.caption: Paragraph 1 introduces the topic. The last sentence states the main idea: every detail points back to it.

teach.h: Finding the main idea in four moves
items: Name the topic in one to three words (here: walking huddles).
Ask what the author says about that topic overall, not in one sentence only.
Check the end of the first paragraph and the last paragraph: a stated main idea usually sits there, but not always.
Test your choice: every supporting detail should fit under it like spokes under an umbrella.

teach.caption: Wrong main-idea options usually miss in one of these two directions.

teach.h: Paragraph main idea vs passage main idea
teach.body: Each paragraph has its own main idea, usually in its topic sentence. The passage has one main idea that covers all the paragraphs; in a HESI A2 passage of 250-500 words it is most often stated in the first paragraph (a thesis) or restated in the last. A stem that says 'the passage' wants the whole-passage idea; 'paragraph 2' wants that paragraph's topic sentence. Answering one with the other is a classic miss.

teach.h: Where a stated main idea usually sits
head: Place
What you find there
Watch for
rows: A new detail or a caveat
teach.caption: Use the location as a lead, then test it: every paragraph must fit under it.

teach.text: The first sentence is not automatically the main idea: it may be a hook, a question or the topic. And a striking statistic is almost never the main idea: it is a supporting detail. On the HESI A2, the 'too narrow' option often copies an exact phrase from the passage, which makes it feel safe.

teach.body: Maya Torres, applying to an ADN program, chose 'Meetings ended on time because no one wanted to keep walking' for the walking-huddle passage. She tested it: does the alertness detail fit under it? No. Does the phone option? No. Does paragraph 3? No. So it is too narrow. 'Exercise improves workplace health' covers far more than the passage says, so it is too broad. The last sentence of paragraph 3 covers every paragraph and nothing extra: that is the main idea.

items: Topic = word or phrase; main idea = the author's point, as a full sentence.
Supporting details are facts, examples, statistics, reasons and anecdotes that prove the point.
A stated main idea is often in the first or last sentence, but a hook can come first.
'The passage' asks for the whole-passage idea; 'paragraph 2' asks for that paragraph's topic sentence.
Reject options that are too narrow (one detail) or too broad (beyond the passage).

summary: You can now separate a passage's topic, main idea and supporting details, and find the sentence that states the main idea of a whole passage or of one paragraph. You can also reject the classic wrong options: a single detail, a claim broader than the passage, and an unrelated true fact.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Public libraries now lend far more than books. In some towns, patrons can borrow blood pressure monitors, telescopes, sewing machines or laptops with the same card they use for novels. Librarians say this 'library of things' helps families who cannot afford equipment they will use only a few times. Items go out for two or three weeks, and staff check each one before it is lent again. In this way, libraries are stretching their old mission of sharing resources to fit modern needs.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Libraries are adapting their sharing mission by lending equipment.
In some towns, patrons can borrow monitors, telescopes and laptops.
Staff inspect each borrowed item before lending it to another patron.
Public libraries have become the most valued service in most towns.
A.why: The last sentence states the point that every detail supports: libraries are extending their mission of sharing by lending useful equipment. The items, the reason (families who cannot afford equipment) and the loan routine all fit under it.

whyNot.1: Too narrow: the list of items is a supporting example, not the point the author makes about it.
whyNot.2: Too narrow: the inspection routine is a minor detail about how the program runs.
whyNot.3: Too broad and unsupported: the passage never compares libraries with other public services.

A.q: A passage argues that street trees lower summer temperatures in city neighborhoods. It cites one block where shade cut sidewalk heat sharply and describes residents who now walk outdoors more. Which choice is the TOPIC of the passage rather than its main idea?
options: Trees cool city neighborhoods in summer
Street trees in city neighborhoods
Shade cut sidewalk heat on one block
Residents now walk outdoors more often
A.why: A topic is a word or phrase naming the subject with no claim attached: 'street trees in city neighborhoods'. The main idea adds what the author says about it.

whyNot.0: This is a complete claim about the topic, so it is the main idea, not the topic.
whyNot.2: This is a supporting detail (one example of the cooling effect).
whyNot.3: This is a supporting detail showing one benefit, not the subject of the passage.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Learning a second language can benefit people at any age. (2) Adults in one community Spanish program said a year of classes made them more confident talking with neighbors. (3) Retirees in the same program said the weekly meetings eased their loneliness. (4) The program was founded in 2015 by a former high school principal. (5) Teenagers who joined reported that the classes helped them understand their grandparents' stories.

Which sentence does NOT support the main idea of the passage?
options: Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 4
A.why: The main idea (sentence 1) is that language learning benefits people of any age. Sentence 4 says who founded the program and when: true within the passage, but it shows no benefit to any learner.

whyNot.0: Sentence 2 shows a benefit for adults: more confidence speaking with neighbors.
whyNot.1: Sentence 3 shows a benefit for retirees: less loneliness.
whyNot.2: Sentence 5 shows a benefit for teenagers, which supports 'at any age'.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Why do so many people feel worn out after a long flight, even when they slept on the plane? Travel fatigue, researchers say, comes less from the hours in the air than from what the cabin does to the body.

(2) Cabin air is kept far drier than the air in most homes, which leaves travelers mildly dehydrated. Long periods of sitting slow circulation in the legs. And crossing time zones confuses the body's internal clock, so sleep comes at the wrong times for days.

What is the main idea of the passage about travel fatigue?
options: Travelers feel tired because they seldom sleep well on planes.
Conditions during air travel, not just flight time, cause fatigue.
Dry cabin air leaves most air travelers mildly dehydrated.
Crossing time zones is the main cause of travel fatigue.
B.why: Paragraph 1 opens with a hook question, then states the thesis: fatigue comes from what the cabin does to the body. Paragraph 2 lists those conditions (dry air, sitting, time zones), and all of them fit under that statement.

whyNot.0: Contradiction: the passage says people feel tired even when they slept on the plane.
whyNot.2: Too narrow: dry air is one of three supporting causes in paragraph 2.
whyNot.3: Too narrow and overstated: time zones are one cause, and the passage never ranks them.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Have you ever wondered why your phone screen seems brighter at night? (2) The screen itself does not change. (3) In a dark room, your pupils widen to let in more light, so the same screen sends more light into your eyes. (4) Your eyes also adjust their sensitivity over several minutes in the dark. (5) The 'brighter' screen, then, is really a change in your eyes, not in the device.

Which sentence states the main idea?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
B.why: Sentence 5 states the conclusion every other sentence builds toward: the apparent brightness comes from the eyes adjusting, not the screen. Sentences 2 to 4 support it.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 is a hook question that introduces the topic; it makes no claim.
whyNot.1: Sentence 3 is one supporting explanation (wider pupils), not the overall point.
whyNot.3: Sentence 2 is a supporting fact; it says what does not change but not why the screen seems brighter.

B.q: A passage reports that employees at a hospital office who took the stairs instead of the elevator for six months had more energy at work and fewer afternoon slumps. A student writes, 'Exercise is good for people,' as the main idea. Why is this a weak choice?
options: It is broader than the passage, which is about taking the stairs at work.
It is narrower than the passage because it describes one employee only.
It repeats one supporting detail instead of the passage's central point.
It names the topic of the passage but leaves out the author's claim.
B.why: The passage makes a specific point about stair climbing at work and energy. 'Exercise is good for people' reaches far beyond what the passage discusses, so it is too broad.

whyNot.1: The statement is general, not about one employee, so it is not too narrow.
whyNot.2: The statement is not a detail from the passage at all; it is a general claim that reaches beyond what the passage reports.
whyNot.3: The statement is a full claim ('is good for people'), so it is not a bare topic; its problem is scope.

C.q:
Read the passage.

For decades, students have been told to study in complete silence. Quiet rooms, the advice goes, protect concentration, and that still holds for some tasks: memorizing drug names or checking a dosage calculation is easier without distraction.

But many learners find that moderate background sound, such as the hum of a cafe, helps them brainstorm and write first drafts. Priya, a nursing student, outlines her papers at a busy coffee shop and edits them later in a silent library. The best study setting, it seems, depends on the kind of thinking a task demands.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the whole passage?
options: Students should study in silence to protect their concentration.
Background noise from a cafe improves every student's writing.
Priya drafts in a coffee shop and edits in a quiet library.
The best place to study depends on the type of task at hand.
C.why: The final sentence pulls both paragraphs together: silence suits some tasks (paragraph 1) and moderate noise suits others (paragraph 2). The main idea is that the right setting depends on the task.

whyNot.0: This states the old advice in paragraph 1, which the passage then qualifies; it covers only the first paragraph.
whyNot.1: Overstatement: the passage says many learners find noise helpful for some tasks, not that it helps every student.
whyNot.2: Too narrow: Priya is one example supporting the main idea.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Community gardens have spread to vacant lots in many American cities. Some grow only flowers; others feed dozens of families each summer.

(2) For many gardeners, the social benefits matter as much as the harvest. Neighbors who had never spoken now trade seeds and recipes. Older residents teach children how to tell when a tomato is ripe. Several gardens host potluck dinners at the end of the season.

(3) City planners have taken notice, and a few cities now set aside public land for new gardens each year.

What is the main idea of paragraph 2 of the community garden passage?
options: Community gardens have spread to vacant city lots.
Older residents teach children to judge ripe tomatoes.
Gardens bring neighbors together as well as feed them.
Cities now set aside public land for new gardens.
C.why: The topic sentence of paragraph 2 says the social benefits matter as much as the harvest; the seed trading, teaching and potlucks all support it.

whyNot.0: Wrong paragraph: this is the point of paragraph 1.
whyNot.1: Too narrow: this is one supporting example inside paragraph 2.
whyNot.3: Wrong paragraph: this is the point of paragraph 3.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) When a patient arrives at an emergency department, someone must decide who is seen first. That job, called triage, usually falls to an experienced nurse.

(2) The triage nurse checks vital signs, asks about symptoms and assigns each patient a level of urgency. A person with chest pain may be taken back at once, while someone with a sprained wrist waits, even if the second person arrived an hour earlier.

(3) To waiting patients, the order can seem unfair. Yet sorting patients by need rather than by arrival time is what allows an emergency department to save the lives most at risk.

What is the main idea of the passage about emergency triage?
options: Triage is usually carried out by an experienced nurse.
Sorting patients by urgency lets the sickest be treated first.
Patients with sprains wait longer than they should in the ER.
Emergency departments should see patients in order of arrival.
C.why: The last sentence states the point the whole passage builds to: sorting by need, not arrival, lets the department save those most at risk. Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain what triage is and how it works.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: who performs triage is a detail from paragraph 1.
whyNot.2: Adds a judgment the author does not make: the author defends the wait.
whyNot.3: Opposite: the author argues for sorting by need rather than arrival time.

reteach.title: Think of an umbrella
reteach.question: Picture an umbrella in the rain with several people huddled under it. Which part is the main idea, which parts are the details, and what is the topic?

blocks.body: The topic is the weather everyone is talking about: rain. The main idea is the umbrella's canopy: one statement big enough to cover every person under it. The supporting details are the people sheltering underneath. If your 'main idea' leaves people standing in the rain, it is too narrow. If it is a giant tent covering the whole street, including people who were never in the passage, it is too broad.

blocks.text: One person under the umbrella is not the umbrella. An answer that repeats one vivid detail word for word is the classic too-narrow trap.

explain.body: The topic is the subject in a word or short phrase, with no claim attached: 'night shift work', 'urban trees', 'library lending'. Ask: what is this passage about?

test.q: A passage explains that school gardens teach children about nutrition, give them outdoor exercise and build teamwork. Which choice is the passage's topic?
options: Gardens help children learn and grow
Children in gardens build teamwork
School gardens
Gardens should be in every school
test.why: The topic is the subject as a phrase with no claim: school gardens.

whyNot.0: This makes a claim about the subject, so it is a main idea, not the topic.
whyNot.3: This is a recommendation the passage does not make, and it is a claim, not a topic.

explain.body: A stated main idea appears in a topic sentence, often the first or last sentence of a paragraph, or the thesis at the end of an introduction. A first sentence may instead be a hook, such as a question, so test every candidate against the details.

steps.label: All fit?
steps.sub: Then it is the main idea

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) What makes a good night of sleep? (2) A consistent bedtime helps set the body's internal clock. (3) A dark, cool room makes falling asleep easier. (4) Avoiding caffeine after noon keeps the mind calmer at night. (5) Simple daily habits, in short, shape how well people sleep.

Which sentence states the main idea?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 5
Sentence 4
test.why: Sentence 5 states the point that sentences 2, 3 and 4 each illustrate: daily habits shape sleep quality.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 is a hook question; it introduces the topic without making a claim.
whyNot.1: Sentence 2 is one supporting habit (consistent bedtime).
whyNot.3: Sentence 4 is one supporting habit (avoiding caffeine).

explain.body: Wrong main-idea options usually miss in scope. Too narrow: one detail, one statistic or one paragraph. Too broad: the general subject area, or a claim reaching beyond the passage. The right answer covers every paragraph and nothing more.

test.q: A passage explains that a city's nurse hotline answers health questions around the clock, steers callers to urgent care instead of the ER when that is safe, and has cut nonurgent ER visits. Which statement is too broad to be the passage's main idea?
options: The hotline has cut nonurgent emergency room visits.
Telephone advice has transformed American health care.
The city's nurse hotline helps callers find the right care.
The hotline answers health questions around the clock.
test.why: The passage is about one city's hotline. A claim about American health care as a whole reaches far beyond it.

whyNot.0: This is too narrow, not too broad: it is one result.
whyNot.2: This is the right-sized main idea: it covers every detail and nothing more.
whyNot.3: This is too narrow, not too broad: it is one feature of the hotline.

explain.body: Read the stem closely. 'The main idea of the passage' covers every paragraph, often stated in the first or last paragraph. 'The main idea of paragraph 1' is that paragraph's topic sentence. The topic sentence of the first paragraph is not always the passage's main idea.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hand sanitizer is convenient, and products with at least 60 percent alcohol kill many germs on hands that are not visibly dirty.

(2) Soap and water, however, work better when hands are visibly dirty or greasy, and they remove some germs that sanitizer does not. Health officials therefore recommend washing with soap and water whenever a sink is available and keeping sanitizer for times when it is not.

What is the main idea of the passage about hand sanitizer?
options: Sanitizer with 60 percent alcohol kills many germs on hands.
Soap and water should replace hand sanitizer in every setting.
Visibly dirty hands are harder to clean than greasy hands.
Soap is preferred when a sink is handy; sanitizer is a backup.
test.why: Paragraph 2 ends with the recommendation that pulls both paragraphs together: wash with soap and water when possible and use sanitizer when not.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: this is the point of paragraph 1 only.
whyNot.1: Overstatement: officials keep sanitizer for times when no sink is available.
whyNot.2: Distortion: the passage groups dirty and greasy hands together; it does not compare them.
